desc:
Two integer arrays a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain repeated values. Return a sorted array of the distinct values that occur in exactly one of the two arrays, that is, in a or in b but not in both.

a = [1, 2, 2, 3, 7]
b = [2, 4, 7, 7, 9]
result = [1, 3, 4, 9]

The value 2 occurs in both arrays and 7 occurs in both, so neither is reported. Each reported value appears once, in strictly increasing order.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Putting both arrays into sets and taking the symmetric difference works, but then you must sort again. Can the sorted order do the work for you?
Sweep with one pointer per array. Compare a[i] and b[j]: the smaller value cannot appear in the other array any more.

If the values differ, the smaller one is exclusive: output it (unless it equals the last output) and skip all copies of it. If they are equal, skip all copies of that value in both arrays. When one array ends, the rest of the other is exclusive.
editorial: Walk two pointers i and j forward. Because both arrays are sorted, if a[i] < b[j] then a[i] is smaller than everything left in b, so it can never be matched: it is an exclusive value. Output it and move i past every copy of that value. Symmetrically for b[j] < a[i]. When the two are equal, the value is shared, so move both pointers past all of its copies and output nothing.

When one array runs out, every remaining distinct value of the other array is exclusive. Skipping whole runs of equal values (or comparing with the last output) keeps the result free of repeats. The algorithm touches each element once, so it runs in O(n + m) time with O(1) extra space beyond the output.
